name: Chrooma Keyboard
platform: Android only (com.gamelounge.chroomakeyboard). No iOS version exists.
vendor: Loopsie SRL (earlier releases under Game Lounge / package com.gamelounge.*; an older package com.frogsparks.mykeyboard is associated with the original developer)
status: Effectively abandoned. Latest tracked releases: helium-5.1.1 (Jun 2020) and hydrogen-2.5.2 (Nov 2023). Still listed on Google Play but unmaintained; some online features reportedly no longer work. Was widely praised in 2016 as one of the year's best Android apps.
evidence_quality: LOW-TO-MEDIUM. Closed source, no SDK, no theme-format documentation, no teardown available, and the app is abandoned so no current vendor material exists. Findings rest on 2016-2020 hands-on reviews and app-store listings. Its value to this research is as a *lightweight, non-image-heavy* theming counter-example, and on that specific axis the evidence is adequate; on packaging/format internals it is near-zero.
rendering_approach:
**Neither per-key bitmaps nor a whole-image background paste — this is a programmatic, color-token-driven renderer, and that is precisely why it is the useful lightweight reference here.** Chrooma's entire theming proposition is that the keyboard is *tinted*, not *skinned*: a small palette is computed or chosen at runtime and applied to programmatically drawn key shapes. There is no theme art to download and, in its core adaptive mode, no background image at all.

Evidence for the tint-not-art model: the keyboard 'adapts its color to the application being used following Google's Material Design guidelines'; the three theme modes are colour-adaptive, fixed-colour and AMOLED (a pure-dark background for OLED panels); users 'add or remove the border around the keys'; and a 'palette styling option displays multiple colors across the keyboard layout to create visual separation between rows.' Every one of those is a property/color operation, not an asset operation. A border toggle and a per-row palette are trivial when keys are drawn shapes and near-impossible when keys are pre-rendered bitmaps.

Per-key differentiation exists but is **role- and row-based, not per-key-addressable**: the row-palette feature colours rows differently, and functional keys are conventionally distinguished from letter keys. There is no evidence of targeting an individual key by code.

Background images: reviews mention colour being 'used for the background image,' which reads as a generated/solid background rather than user photo wallpaper; no source describes importing a gallery photo as a keyboard background. [uncertain] The safest characterisation is: **solid/derived colour fill behind programmatically drawn, optionally-bordered key shapes** — the lightest-weight approach of the three items studied.
selector_and_state_model:
[uncertain] No author-facing rule syntax exists — Chrooma has no theme file, no stylesheet, and no third-party theme authoring at all. Themes are app-internal modes plus user colour choices, so there is nothing resembling a selector language, cascade, or specificity model. This is the opposite end of the spectrum from FlorisBoard's `key[code=..]:pressed`.

What the renderer plausibly distinguishes internally:
- **normal / pressed** — universal; a pressed key visual and key-preview popup exist.
- **key role** — functional keys (shift, delete, symbols, enter) versus letter keys are conventionally tinted differently under Material Design, and the accent/action key typically takes the primary colour.
- **row index** — uniquely evidenced here: the palette-styling option colours rows differently 'to create visual separation between rows.' Row is an unusual selector dimension and is worth noting as a cheap way to add visual richness without per-key art.
- **border on/off** — a global toggle rather than a per-key selector.
- **theme mode** — adaptive / fixed / AMOLED, plus night mode, act as top-level variants that swap the whole palette.
- **per-app override** — the genuinely distinctive dimension: a user can 'set a custom color for each app,' so the effective 'selector' includes *the foreground application package*. No other keyboard studied here treats app identity as a theming input.

Shift/caps state, disabled and focus states are not evidenced as separately themeable. [uncertain — all internal-model detail is inferred]
rendering_pipeline:
[uncertain] A custom `View` with `Canvas`/`Drawable` rendering inside an `InputMethodService`, near-certainly derived from the **AOSP LatinIME** codebase. Direct confirmation of the fork was not found, but the circumstantial case is strong: contemporary reviews repeatedly note Chrooma 'closely mirrors Google's stock offering' and provides 'a very similar experience to the Google Keyboard' while adding features Google hadn't; it shipped gesture typing, a number-row toggle, one-hand mode and split layout — the standard LatinIME feature surface; and its 2016-era origins predate Jetpack Compose entirely. AOSP LatinIME draws all keys in a single custom `KeyboardView.onDraw()` and repaints individual keys via `invalidateKey()`, which is exactly the pipeline that makes runtime tinting cheap.

Per-keystroke cost is low by construction: with no bitmaps to decode and only colour values changing, a theme switch is a palette swap plus invalidate, and a key press repaints one key's rect. This is the performance argument for the lightweight approach — the whole theme is a handful of ints.

The interesting cost is elsewhere: **detecting the foreground app to drive adaptive colour**. Reviews describe the transition happening 'all automatically as you jump between each without a hiccup,' so it is fast, but one reviewer notes 'rapid color changes' can feel 'jarring, particularly in low-light conditions' — a UX cost, not a frame cost. Compose-in-IME lifecycle blockers do not apply since Compose almost certainly isn't used. [uncertain: no code-level confirmation; the LatinIME lineage is inferred, and one search explicitly failed to confirm it]
compositing_scrim_model:
[uncertain] **Essentially no compositing stack — and that is the finding.** With no background photograph there is nothing to scrim: the layer model reduces to a solid or derived background colour, key shapes drawn over it with optional borders, and labels on top. No dim overlay, no brightness slider, no blur, and no opacity control is described in any source — none of which are needed when the background is a flat colour the app itself chose, because legibility can be guaranteed by construction rather than by user correction.

This is the clean architectural contrast with Facemoji, which *must* ship brightness and key-opacity sliders because it pastes arbitrary user photos behind the keys. Chrooma sidesteps the entire legibility-over-imagery problem by never introducing imagery.

One partial exception: the **RGB theme** (premium, added ~2019) renders 'a wave of color across the keyboard' in motion, which implies a gradient or per-key colour-cycling layer composited over or into the key layer. Whether that is a gradient shader across the key grid or per-key colour interpolation is undocumented. [uncertain]

Night mode operates as a palette shift (darkening the colour tone), not as an overlay scrim. [uncertain: could plausibly be implemented as a dark overlay, but the description — 'change automatically the color tone' — reads as palette substitution]. No concrete opacity or alpha values are published anywhere.
asset_types:
**Minimal to none for theming — the defining characteristic of this item.** There is no theme art: no 9-patch key bitmaps, no downloadable wallpapers, no per-density drawable sets for theme content. Keys are drawn shapes (likely XML shape drawables or direct `Canvas` primitives with `Paint`), so a 'theme' is a set of colour integers plus a few boolean flags (border on/off, AMOLED, night mode).

Consequences worth carrying forward: (a) themes cost effectively zero bytes and zero decode time, so there is no per-theme download, no storage growth, and no bitmap memory; (b) density bucketing is irrelevant because nothing is rastered — everything is dp-based and resolution-independent; (c) the whole app is 23.36 MB (helium-5.1.1) *including* emoji and GIF features, versus Facemoji's 34.1 MB plus per-theme downloads.

The only theme-adjacent raster assets are app chrome and emoji glyph sets (the app offers iOS/iPhone/Android emoji styles), which are product assets rather than theme assets. [uncertain: exact drawing mechanism — XML shape drawables versus direct Canvas — is inferred]
theme_package_manifest_format:
[uncertain] **No theme package format exists, as far as any available evidence shows.** Chrooma has no theme marketplace, no downloadable theme files, no import/export, and no third-party theme authoring — it is not a theme-distribution product at all, which is exactly why it sits in this research as the lightweight counter-example rather than as a marketplace comparator.

What is persisted instead is almost certainly plain app preferences: a theme-mode enum (adaptive / fixed / AMOLED), a chosen accent or fixed colour, border on/off, night-mode settings and schedule, keyboard scale percentage, custom spacebar text, and a **per-app colour override map** (package name → colour) which is the only structured data of any complexity. `SharedPreferences` plus perhaps a small SQLite/Room table for the per-app map is the expected implementation.

No manifest, no folder layout, no ZIP, no plugin APK. Premium themes (including RGB) are unlocked by in-app purchase rather than downloaded, meaning they ship inside the APK and are gated by an entitlement flag rather than delivered as content. [uncertain: all persistence detail is inferred; no teardown available]
token_count_tiering:
[uncertain] No published token count, and the honest answer is that the number is **small — plausibly under 10 core colour tokens** rather than the couple dozen of a marketplace schema or FlorisBoard's 24 properties × ~90 elements.

Reasoning from what the UI exposes: a Material-Design-derived palette needs roughly primary/accent, keyboard background, key background, key text, functional-key background, and a secondary/variant — six-ish values — from which everything else is derived. The row-palette feature suggests a small ordered list of row colours derived from the primary rather than independently authored. Marketing claims 'over ten thousand customizations,' but that is a combinatorial count across all settings (layout, size, behaviour, language, gestures), not a theming token count, and should not be read as such.

**Tiering is by monetisation, not by complexity** — an important distinction from Facemoji's simple-vs-advanced authoring tiers. Free tier: adaptive / fixed / AMOLED modes, night mode, per-app colours, border toggle. Premium tier (a $4.99 in-app purchase): the RGB theme, other premium themes, keyboard size adjustment, disabling the action row, and further appearance options. So the paywall gates *which* appearance features you may use, not *how deeply* you may author. [uncertain: token count is estimated, not documented]
theme_versioning_forward_compat:
[uncertain] Not applicable in any meaningful sense — with no theme file format there is no schema to version and no forward-compatibility problem to solve. This is a genuine architectural advantage of the token/tint approach worth noting explicitly: **a colour-token theme model has no theme-file compatibility surface at all**, so adding new appearance settings over time cannot break anything a user previously configured; unset preferences simply take new defaults. Compare FlorisBoard, where the Snygg v1 → v2 transition hard-broke every existing theme with no upgrade path, and Facemoji, where a server-side catalogue must stay compatible with old clients.

The residual risk is ordinary preference migration across app updates (a renamed preference key losing a user's saved colours), and given the app's abandoned state — the release naming itself shifted lineage from `helium-*` to `hydrogen-*`, suggesting at least one significant rewrite — some user-settings loss across that boundary is plausible. Unverified.
color_extraction_dynamic_tinting:
**This is Chrooma's entire reason for existing and the field with the most substantive evidence.** The keyboard performs runtime dynamic tinting keyed to the **foreground application**, which is a colour-source no other item in this study uses. Confirmed behaviour: 'the keyboard changes its color and theme based on the app the user is currently using' — green in Hangouts, red in Gmail, yellow in Keep — following Material Design guidelines, toggled via 'Adapt keyboard color' in the Appearance tab. It also colours the system **navigation bar** to match the current app.

The three modes are: **colour-adaptive** (per-app), **fixed colour** (user picks one), and **AMOLED** (pure dark for OLED). Users may additionally 'set a custom color for each app,' i.e. override the automatic derivation per package.

**The derivation mechanism is not documented anywhere** [uncertain] and reviews are conspicuously vague, one attributing it to 'artificial intelligence' (marketing language, not a mechanism). The realistic candidates are: (a) a curated lookup table mapping popular package names to their known brand colours — which would explain the pinpoint accuracy on Hangouts/Gmail/Keep and the instant, hiccup-free switching; (b) runtime extraction from the app's launcher icon via the Android **Palette API**; (c) reading the foreground app's status-bar/primary colour. A hybrid — curated table for popular apps, Palette-on-icon fallback for the long tail — is the most plausible design and is what I would expect a reimplementation to need.

Note what this is *not*: it is **not** Material You. Chrooma's adaptive colour predates Android 12 by five years and derives from the foreground app, whereas Material You derives from the system wallpaper (which is what FlorisBoard uses). These are different sources solving different problems, and Chrooma's is arguably the more interesting one for a keyboard, since the keyboard is always seen adjacent to some other app's UI.

A secondary dynamic input is **ambient light**: night mode 'change[s] automatically the color tone when low light is detected,' plus a user-programmable timer/schedule — so the light sensor is a second runtime tinting input. [uncertain: sensor vs. time-of-day implementation detail]
contrast_enforcement_accessibility:
[uncertain] No explicit contrast validation, WCAG/APCA checking, or accessibility conformance claim appears in any source. But Chrooma's architecture **structurally avoids most of the legibility problem** rather than solving it explicitly, and the distinction matters:

- Colours are derived under **Material Design guidelines**, which are themselves contrast-aware — Material's colour system pairs each surface colour with an 'on-' colour chosen for legibility, so following the guideline yields acceptable label contrast largely for free. If the implementation genuinely derives an on-colour per surface (rather than hardcoding white labels), contrast is handled implicitly.
- There is **no background photograph**, so the pathological case — text over a busy image — never arises. This single decision eliminates the failure mode that forces Facemoji to ship brightness/opacity sliders and that Snygg leaves entirely to the theme author.
- **Night mode** with automatic low-light detection is an accessibility-adjacent feature: it reduces glare and eye strain in dim conditions, and the reviewer complaint that rapid colour changes are 'jarring, particularly in low-light conditions' shows the vendor was engaging with exactly this axis.
- **Key borders are a user-controllable toggle**, which is the classic legibility escape hatch — and notably it is exposed to the *end user*, not just to a theme author. FlorisBoard treats borderless-vs-bordered as an author-chosen theme variant; Chrooma lets the user force borders on regardless of theme.
- **AMOLED mode** provides a guaranteed maximum-contrast dark option.

Unknown: whether any minimum-contrast clamp is applied when a user picks an arbitrary fixed or per-app colour. A user free-picking a pale yellow could plausibly produce illegible white labels, and nothing suggests the app prevents it. [uncertain]
background_geometry_adaptation:
**Largely a non-issue by design — the strongest practical argument for the lightweight approach.** With a solid or derived colour fill rather than a raster background, there is nothing to crop, letterbox, stretch, or re-author per geometry. A colour is resolution-, aspect-ratio- and size-independent, so the same theme is pixel-correct at any keyboard height, in portrait or landscape, on phone or tablet, with no per-orientation assets. Compare the documented commercial norm of shipping **separate portrait and landscape wallpapers** per theme, and the crop-quality problems an arbitrary user photo faces across those geometries.

Chrooma exercises a wide range of geometries and handles them without theme-side complication: **keyboard scaling in 10% increments**, **one-hand mode**, **split layout** for larger devices, and a **number-row toggle**. Each changes the key grid substantially; none requires theme rework, because keys are drawn shapes that lay out at whatever size the layout engine assigns.

The premium **RGB theme** is the one case with real geometry dependence — a colour wave travelling across the key grid must be parameterised by grid extent — but as a generated effect it can be computed for whatever grid exists rather than authored per geometry. [uncertain: RGB implementation detail]

Floating-mode behaviour is not documented. [uncertain]
layout_locale_independence:
Strong, essentially for free. With no positional art and no fixed key-grid bitmap, layout changes cannot break the theme: toggling the number row, switching to AZERTY/QWERTZ/Dvorak or a non-Latin script, enabling split layout, or mirroring for RTL all just change how many key shapes are laid out and where — each still drawn from the same colour tokens. Chrooma explicitly supports multilingual typing without keyboard switching, plus one-hand and split layouts, and no source mentions any theme incompatibility across them, which is consistent.

The row-palette feature is the only mildly layout-coupled element: colouring by row index behaves sensibly as long as the layout is row-structured, which all standard layouts are, but the visual rhythm would shift if row count changed (e.g. number row on/off adds a row and thus shifts the palette assignment). This degrades gracefully — it still looks intentional — rather than breaking. [uncertain: how row colours are assigned when row count changes]

Custom spacebar text is a small locale-adjacent feature (user-defined text on the spacebar) but is user content, not theme art.
non_key_surface_coverage:
[uncertain] Coverage is **broad but shallow** — the tint propagates everywhere automatically because it is a palette rather than a set of authored surfaces, which is a real advantage of the token approach: you get consistent theming of new surfaces for free as the app grows, with no per-surface art to commission.

Confirmed or strongly implied surfaces:
- **System navigation bar** — explicitly confirmed: a 'colored navbar that changes with your current app.' This is notable because it reaches *outside* the keyboard's own bounds, and neither FlorisBoard nor Facemoji is documented as doing it. It presumably uses `Window.setNavigationBarColor` on the IME window.
- **Action row / toolbar** — confirmed to exist as a themed element (disabling it is a premium feature).
- **Suggestion/prediction strip** — near-certain; contextual predictions are a headline feature and the strip sits within the tinted keyboard surface.
- **Emoji and GIF panels** — the app has integrated emoji, GIF search and multiple emoji glyph styles; these panels would inherit the palette. [uncertain]
- **Key-preview popup and long-press mini-keyboard** — implied by the pressed-state machinery. [uncertain]
- **One-hand-mode side panel and split-layout chrome** — implied by the features existing. [uncertain]
- **Settings/clipboard sheets** — not evidenced. [uncertain]

The trade-off versus FlorisBoard: Chrooma likely tints ~all surfaces uniformly, whereas Snygg exposes ~90 individually addressable named elements. Uniform coverage is cheaper and more consistent; per-element addressing is more expressive.
sound_haptic_theming:
[uncertain] **Not themed.** No source describes key sounds or haptics as part of a Chrooma theme, and this is consistent with the architecture — a theme here is a colour palette, and there is no theme package that could carry an audio asset. Key-press sound and vibration almost certainly exist as ordinary global user preferences (universal in this app class, and inherited directly if the codebase descends from AOSP LatinIME, which has exactly these settings), but they are settings rather than theme-carried properties.

This matches FlorisBoard's boundary (visual-only themes) and contrasts with Facemoji, where themed key-press sounds are a marketed, per-theme feature. The lesson for a theming product: sound-as-part-of-theme is a marketplace differentiator, and both non-marketplace keyboards studied here omit it.

Expected underlying APIs on Android, if reimplementing: `SoundPool` or `AudioManager.playSoundEffect(FX_KEYPRESS_*)` for sound, `HapticFeedbackConstants.KEYBOARD_TAP` via `View.performHapticFeedback()` or `Vibrator`/`VibratorManager` for haptics, with respect for the system's keypress sound/vibrate settings. [uncertain: unverified for this specific app]
platform_apis_frameworks:
[uncertain] Android-only, and a fairly classic pre-Compose Android stack. Expected components: `InputMethodService` as host; a custom `KeyboardView`-style `View` with `Canvas`/`Paint`/`Drawable` rendering, most likely descended from **AOSP LatinIME**; XML shape drawables and/or `GradientDrawable` for key shapes with runtime colour setting; `ColorStateList`/`setColorFilter`/`setTint` for the actual tinting; `Window.setNavigationBarColor` for the coloured navbar.

For the adaptive-colour feature specifically, the interesting API question is **how the foreground app is detected** — historically via `ActivityManager.getRunningTasks()` (deprecated), `UsageStatsManager` (requires the PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS special access), or — most likely for an IME and requiring no permission at all — reading `EditorInfo.packageName` from `onStartInputView()`, which hands the IME the package of the app it is typing into. That last route is almost certainly what Chrooma uses: it is free, instant, permission-less, and would explain the 'without a hiccup' switching. [uncertain but high-confidence inference]. Colour derivation would then use either a bundled package→colour table or `androidx.palette.graphics.Palette` over the app's icon fetched via `PackageManager.getApplicationIcon()`.

Night mode's low-light detection implies `SensorManager` with `TYPE_LIGHT`. [uncertain]

No Material You / `DynamicColors` (predates it), no Jetpack Compose, no iOS frameworks (no iOS build exists).
delivery_installation_pipeline:
**All themes are bundled in the APK — there is no delivery pipeline, and that is the point.** No downloadable themes, no theme store, no import/export, no plugin APKs, no server dependency for appearance. Free themes (adaptive, fixed, AMOLED, night mode) and premium themes (RGB and others) all ship inside the 23.36 MB application; premium ones are unlocked by a $4.99 in-app purchase that flips an entitlement rather than downloading content. Nothing theme-related lands on disk beyond preference values.

Operational consequences, all favourable and all relevant to evaluating a lightweight approach: zero theme CDN or hosting cost, zero download latency when switching themes (instant, since it's a palette swap), no per-theme storage growth, no offline degradation, no untrusted-content ingestion path, and no store-policy exposure around runtime-downloaded content. The corresponding cost is the obvious one — the catalogue is fixed at ship time and cannot grow without an app update, which is commercially fatal for a themes-as-a-product business and is precisely why marketplace keyboards accept the complexity Chrooma avoided.

Distribution is Google Play (plus APKMirror/Uptodown mirrors). Given the app is abandoned, some online features reportedly no longer work, though bundled theming should be unaffected by server decay — an incidental durability benefit of bundling. [uncertain: whether any premium theme content was ever server-delivered]
permission_store_policy_surface:
[uncertain] Very low surface — materially lower than either comparator, and a direct consequence of not downloading content.

- **No iOS considerations at all**: Android-only, so Full Access / `RequestsOpenAccess` and the App Store's keyboard-extension review scrutiny simply do not apply. This is the single biggest difference from Facemoji.
- **Android IME enablement** is the only mandatory step; theming needs no additional runtime permission because there is no image import, no external storage access for theme content, and no network fetch for appearance.
- **No downloaded-executable-code concern**: nothing is downloaded, so Play's restrictions on runtime code delivery are moot. Marketplace keyboards must carefully keep theme payloads inert to stay compliant; Chrooma has no such obligation.
- **Possible special access for foreground-app detection**: if the adaptive feature used `UsageStatsManager`, it would require the PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS special access grant — a notable UX friction. But as argued under platform_apis_frameworks, `EditorInfo.packageName` is the more likely and permission-free route, and no source mentions a usage-access prompt, which supports the permission-free reading. [uncertain]
- **Keyboards remain a heightened-scrutiny Play category** (they can observe all typed input) with data-safety disclosure obligations, independent of theming.
- **Light sensor** access for night mode requires no permission on Android.
memory_performance_budget:
**The lightest budget of the three items, by a wide margin, and the clearest demonstration of what the non-image-heavy approach buys you.** No explicit ceiling is documented [uncertain] — and none is needed, because there is essentially nothing to budget: a theme is a handful of colour integers and boolean flags. Concretely, the theming subsystem contributes ~zero heap: no decoded bitmaps, no per-key drawable cache, no background image, no eviction policy required, no downsampling logic, no `OutOfMemoryError` risk from oversized user photos.

The app is marketed as 'lightweight, fast' and ships at **23.36 MB** total (helium-5.1.1) *including* emoji and GIF features — versus Facemoji's 34.1 MB plus per-theme downloads plus resident background bitmaps.

Android imposes no hard IME memory ceiling comparable to the **iOS keyboard extension's ~30-40 MB dirty / ~77 MB total** limit, so Chrooma never faced that constraint. But the relevant hypothetical is instructive: **this architecture would comfortably fit inside the iOS extension budget**, whereas an image-per-theme architecture struggles there. For any product that must ship an iOS keyboard, the colour-token approach is the one that fits without heroics.

Runtime cost is a palette swap plus a view invalidate on theme change, and a single-key repaint on press. The one genuine ongoing cost is the **premium RGB theme's continuous colour-wave animation**, which is real per-frame work and a battery consideration; no frame-rate cap or idle-pause behaviour is documented for it. [uncertain]
untrusted_theme_validation_security:
**Effectively no attack surface — because there is no untrusted theme content.** Themes are bundled in the signed APK and are not downloaded, imported, or user-supplied as files, so the entire class of risks that a theme marketplace inherits simply does not exist here: no ZIP extraction and therefore no zip-slip/path-traversal exposure, no untrusted image decoding and therefore no decompression-bomb DoS, no third-party manifest parsing and therefore no malformed-manifest handling to get wrong, no custom font files hitting native font parsers, and no theme-payload signing problem to solve.

The only untrusted-ish inputs are user-chosen colour values and per-app colour overrides, which are trivially validated (a colour int is a colour int) and cannot carry a payload.

This is worth stating positively rather than as an absence: it is a real security property of the architecture, and it is the mirror image of the FlorisBoard finding, where the existence of downloadable `.flex` files necessitated explicit path-canonicalisation defences in `FlorisAssetResolver`. If a product does not need a theme marketplace, declining to build one removes an entire threat class.

Residual concern is unrelated to theming: the app is abandoned and unpatched since 2023, so any latent vulnerability elsewhere in a keyboard — an app that by definition sees every keystroke — will never be fixed. That is a genuine reason not to recommend running it today. [uncertain: no security audit of the app exists]
open_source_reference_availability:
**No source available.** Chrooma is fully closed source with no public repository, no theme SDK, no format documentation, and no developer-facing material of any kind. The app is additionally abandoned, so no vendor documentation is being maintained and the developer is unresponsive — there is no route to clarification by asking.

A targeted search to confirm the widely-assumed **AOSP LatinIME** derivation returned no confirmation, so even the lineage is inference rather than fact, though the feature surface and review commentary ('a very similar experience to the Google Keyboard') support it. If the derivation is real, then AOSP LatinIME itself is the best available proxy for the rendering pipeline — it is Apache-2.0 and readable, with several maintained forks (e.g. `leonardoquevedox/AOSP-LatinIME`, `marcosdiez/aosp-morelang-ime`, and the `HeliBoard`/`OpenBoard` lineage which is the actively maintained modern descendant and a far better study target than Chrooma itself).

The only route to Chrooma's actual internals is decompiling an APK (`com.gamelounge.chroomakeyboard`, 23.36 MB, available on APKMirror/Uptodown), where the interesting artefacts would be any bundled package-name→colour lookup table (which would settle the colour-derivation question) and the key-drawing code. **For studying lightweight token-based keyboard theming with real source, HeliBoard/OpenBoard is the recommended substitute.**
authoring_tooling_preview_generation:
[uncertain] **No theme authoring tooling exists** — there is no theme editor, no external toolchain, no export/import, and no way for a user or third party to author and distribute a theme. What exists is a settings surface, not an editor: an Appearance tab with an 'Adapt keyboard color' toggle, theme-mode selection (adaptive / fixed / AMOLED), a colour picker for fixed mode, per-app colour assignment, a key-border toggle, night-mode configuration with a schedule, keyboard scaling in 10% increments, action-row visibility (premium), and custom spacebar text.

Live preview: not explicitly documented, but essentially inherent — changes are palette swaps applied instantly, and the keyboard is visible while configuring in most such apps. [uncertain]

**No store thumbnail or preview-variant generation requirement**, because there is no store. This contrasts sharply with the marketplace model, where the documented commercial norm is three rendered previews per theme (large with borders, large without borders, small) plus portrait and landscape wallpapers — a per-theme asset-production burden that Chrooma's approach eliminates entirely. For a themes-as-a-product business this is the hidden cost that the lightweight approach avoids: every marketplace theme needs authored art *and* multiple authored preview renders.
cross_platform_token_parity:
**Not applicable — Android only, no iOS version has ever existed.** So there is no cross-platform theme definition and no parity to assess empirically.

The conceptual answer is more useful, and it is favourable: because a Chrooma-style theme is nothing but a small set of colour values plus boolean flags, it is **the most trivially portable of the three models studied**. A palette of six-or-so colours plus border/AMOLED/night flags maps onto SwiftUI or UIKit without loss — there are no 9-patch assets to re-encode (the sticking point for Facemoji's key art), no `flex://` asset resolution, and no platform-specific dynamic-colour dependency. A single shared JSON of colour tokens could drive both platforms verbatim.

The genuinely platform-bound pieces are behavioural rather than visual:
- **Foreground-app detection** to drive adaptive colour: on Android an IME reads `EditorInfo.packageName`; on iOS a keyboard extension **cannot reliably identify the host app** — there is no supported API for it. The adaptive-colour feature, Chrooma's entire premise, is therefore **not implementable on iOS**. This is the key portability finding.
- **Navigation-bar colouring** has no iOS equivalent.
- **Ambient-light-driven night mode**: iOS keyboard extensions have no light-sensor access; the closest substitute is the system light/dark appearance trait, which is a different (and simpler) input.

So: the *token format* ports perfectly; the *dynamic behaviour that makes the tokens interesting* does not.
animation_budget:
[uncertain] **Flag as weakly documented.** Animation exists but is confined to one premium feature. The **RGB theme** (introduced ~April 2019, premium, part of the $4.99 unlock) renders a continuously moving 'wave of color' across the keyboard, likened to an RGB gaming keyboard's lighting sweep. A reviewer confirms it is genuinely animated — 'what doesn't translate well via a photo is the motion the RGB theme performs when enabled' — and describes it as 'trippy and mildly distracting at first' though ultimately pleasant in normal use.

Everything unspecified: the implementation (per-key colour interpolation on a timer versus an animated gradient shader across the key grid), the frame rate or any cap, whether the animation pauses when the keyboard is idle rather than being typed on, and its battery impact. None of these are addressed in any source, and there is no vendor documentation to consult. Given the app's abandoned state these questions can only be answered empirically or by decompilation.

What can be said architecturally: because the animation is **generated rather than asset-driven** — no Lottie, no GIF, no video, no frame sequence — it costs essentially nothing in memory and download size, unlike an animated-background theme in a marketplace keyboard. The cost is purely CPU/GPU per frame while visible. That is a meaningfully different trade: procedural animation is memory-cheap and battery-expensive, asset animation is both memory- and battery-expensive. For an iOS keyboard extension living inside ~40 MB, procedural animation is the only viable kind. Idle-pause remains the open question that would determine whether it is acceptable in practice.

color_extraction_dynamic_tinting (per-app adaptive colour — extensively reviewed; only the derivation mechanism is unknown)
delivery_installation_pipeline (no theme store; all bundled, premium unlocked by IAP)
cross_platform_token_parity (Android-only; no iOS build has ever existed)
key_takeaway_for_lightweight_theming: Chrooma demonstrates that a keyboard theme can be ~6 colour tokens plus a few flags and still feel highly customised, because the perceived richness comes from *dynamic derivation* (per-app colour, ambient-light night mode) and from cheap structural variation (row palettes, border toggle, AMOLED variant) rather than from authored art. The cascading benefits are large and mutually reinforcing: no theme packaging format, no versioning/compat surface, no asset pipeline, no per-orientation art, no download infrastructure, no untrusted-content threat class, no preview-render production burden, near-zero memory, and trivial cross-platform token portability. The costs are equally clear: the catalogue cannot grow without an app update, so a themes-as-a-product marketplace is impossible; expressive art-driven themes (the entire Facemoji proposition) are off the table; and the one feature that made it special — per-app adaptive colour — is not implementable on iOS, since a keyboard extension cannot identify its host app.
